These systems have developed rapidly over the past 40 years or so, taking advantage of the increase in available computing power, of new algorithms and of the use of fluorescent DNA stains. Their purpose is to increase the objectivity and accuracy of semen analysis, since they largely remove the human factor from the process. As well as measuring sperm concentration, morphology and motility, these analysers also allow the calculation of kinematic parameters that are absent from the standard semen analysis, such as curvilinear velocity (VCL) and straight-line velocity (VSL). Each analyser is also linked to software, allowing the data to be organized and analysed statistically. Their disadvantages include unreliable measurements for samples with a low (< 2 × 10⁶/ml) or very high concentration (> 50 × 10⁶/ml), and for dirty samples containing many cells that are not sperm. Although more research is needed to demonstrate their benefits in andrology laboratories, these systems are useful for laboratory quality control.
